- **Identification.** No source uses the exact label "7-Phase Debugging Workflow". The established seven-step debugging process is Andreas Zeller's **TRAFFIC** method (Track, Reproduce, Automate, Find origins, Focus, Isolate, Correct), from *Why Programs Fail* (Morgan Kaufmann, 1st ed. 2005; 2nd ed. 2009). This report treats the concept as TRAFFIC. https://www.embedded.com/a-guide-to-systematic-program-debugging-part-1/ - **Rejected readings.** The "seven stages of debugging" meme (shock, denial, and so on) is a joke about emotions, not a workflow: https://blog.vivekhaldar.com/post/23162993767

18. Zeller's later open textbook, *The Debugging Book*, does not organise its introduction around TRAFFIC. It uses a five-step scientific-method loop instead: question, hypothesis, prediction, experiment, repeat. It cites *Why Programs Fail* (2009) only as background for "systematic debugging processes". — https://www.debuggingbook.org/html/Intro_Debugging.html (last modified 2024-10-15) 19. Practitioner writing still presents TRAFFIC as a "general debugging workflow" and credits it to Zeller. — https://symflower.com/en/company/blog/2023/debugging-with-the-traffic-principle/ (22 Feb 2023) 20.

1. Zeller states that debugging "can be decomposed into seven steps of which the initial letters form the word TRAFFIC." — https://www.embedded.com/a-guide-to-systematic-program-debugging-part-1/ 2. The seven steps are: Track the problem in the database; Reproduce the failure; Automate and simplify the test case; Find possible infection origins; Focus on the most likely origins; Isolate the infection chain; Correct the defect. — https://www.embedded.com/a-guide-to-systematic-program-debugging-part-1/ 3. Zeller's own lecture slides "How Failures Come to be" label the list "The Traffic Principle

TRAFFIC rests on Zeller's defect → infection → failure chain: the programmer creates a defect (an error in the code), running it creates an infection (an error in the state), the infection propagates, and the infection causes a failure. — https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/HowFailuresComeToBe.pdf (slide 12) 7. The slides state that "This infection chain must be traced back – and broken." — https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/HowFailuresComeToBe.pdf (slide 12) 8. Zeller defines debugging as relating a given failure to its defect and then removing the defect. — https://www.whyprogramsfail.co

10. Just before introducing TRAFFIC, the slides show a four-step debugging model attributed to Sommerville (2004): Locate error → Design error repair → Repair error → Re-test program. TRAFFIC expands this by adding tracking, reproduction and automation before localisation. — https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/HowFailuresComeToBe.pdf (slide 9) 11. The Automate and Isolate steps build on Zeller's delta debugging, which he developed at Saarland University in 1999 and first published as "Yesterday, my program worked. Today, it does not. Why?" (ESEC/FSE '99). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_

1. A failure happens in three stages. The programmer creates a *defect*. The defect causes an *infection*. The infection causes a *failure*, which is an error you can see from outside. https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/HowFailuresComeToBe.pdf 2. Definitions: defect = wrong program code; infection = wrong program state; failure = wrong behaviour you can observe. https://www.embedded.com/a-guide-to-systematic-program-debugging-part-1/ 3. The debuggingbook adds a stage before the defect: Mistake (a human act) → Defect → Fault (another name for infection) → Failure. https://www.debuggingbook.org

**R — Reproduce** 15. Reproduction is "the first task" after a report or a failing test. It does two jobs. It lets you observe the problem ("without being able to reproduce the problem, one cannot observe it or find any new facts"). It lets you check whether a fix worked. https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/ReproducingProblems.pdf 16. Reproduction has two parts. You recreate the *environment*, and you recreate the *problem history*, meaning the steps that led to the problem. Zeller calls reproducing "one of the toughest problems in debugging." https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/ReproducingPro

**A — Automate (and simplify)** 21. Automate the failure-provoking test, so that each later experiment and fix check needs no manual re-runs. https://symflower.com/en/company/blog/2023/debugging-with-the-traffic-principle/ 22. Simplify the test mechanically with Delta Debugging. Delta Debugging reduces a failing test case to a minimal one that still fails. It can also isolate the difference between a passing and a failing test case. https://www.st.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/details/zeller-tse-2002/ 23. Published effect sizes: 95 Mozilla user actions reduced to 3, and 896 lines of HTML red

45. Delta Debugging, and so step A, assumes a test that is deterministic and fast. https://www.debuggingbook.org/html/DeltaDebugger.html 46. Iterative reproduction ends either when the failure appears or when the environments are "identical". In the second case, the failure may still not reproduce. https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/ReproducingProblems.pdf 47. Capturing the environment is expensive: millions of configurations and dozens of test machines. Recording communication hurts performance. User data raises privacy issues. https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/ReproducingProblems.pdf 48.

1. Zeller's TRAFFIC method has seven steps. Their initials spell TRAFFIC: "Track the problem in the database. Reproduce the failure. Automate and simplify the test case. Find possible infection origins. Focus on the most likely origins. Isolate the infection chain. Correct the defect." — https://www.embedded.com/a-guide-to-systematic-program-debugging-part-1/ 2. 27. What follows from claims 18–20 and 23–24: the phase that pays off most is producing and ranking explicit hypotheses. Just locating the fault ("Isolate"/"Trace" without a hypothesis) showed no benefit in a controlled experiment. — https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.13652 28. What follows from claims 21–22: the seven phases do not describe what developers actually observe doing. Real episodes mix activities without a set order. - **Linear phases vs how professionals actually debug.** TRAFFIC is presented as an ordered list. A 2026 grounded-theory study of professional debugging (Li and Coblenz) found an *iterative* process instead. In it, developers keep updating a mental model and alternate between navigation and execution strategies and between forward and backward tracing. The study does not cite TRAFFIC. It contradicts a strictly sequential reading of the phases, not the phases themselves. — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11435 - **Zeller's own framing has shifted.** In 2005 and 2009 he led with TRAFFIC's seven steps

25. Li & Coblenz (arXiv 2602.11435, 2026) describe professional debugging as iterative: developers "cycle through debugging, implementing a fix, and validating the fix." — https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11435v1 26. In that study, "In 9 out of the 17 tasks, a participant returned to the mental model update step after testing an initial fix." That is a loop back from Phase 7 to Phase 5, which the linear 7-phase ordering does not model. — https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11435v1 27. The same study measured the time split as 12% reproducing, 57% updating the mental model, 13% fixing and 18% validating. Un

- **D1 — Linear steps vs. iterative practice.** TRAFFIC is presented as "proceed in 7 steps" (https://www.whyprogramsfail.com/pdf/HowFailuresComeToBe.pdf). A grounded-theory study of 12 professionals on 17 real tasks (Li & Coblenz, arXiv, 2026-02-11) found debugging to be "a structured, iterative diagnostic process" that adapts to the codebase context, complexity and familiarity, rather than following a fixed sequence (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11435). Other "7 stages/steps of debugging" material is either an emotional taxonomy or undated SEO lists with no original source (see Disagreements). This report treats "7-Phase Debugging Workflow" as TRAFFIC unless the concept-tree node says otherwise.

1. **Primary:** Andreas Zeller's TRAFFIC method. Its seven steps are Track, Reproduce, Automate, Find, Focus, Isolate, Correct. 2. **Recent:** seven-step debugging skills for AI coding agents, for example Reproduce → Isolate → Trace → Hypothesize → Test → Fix → Verify.
**Evaluation evidence:** only empirical work that tests the workflow's assumptions: phase order, hypothesis-driven search, and isolation before fixing.

**Out of scope:** sibling techniques such as delta debugging, fault localization, printf debugging and rubber-ducking, the wider Debugging Techniques domain, and other debugging frameworks. These are named only where a claim needs them as a contrast.
